html:
A late Bronze Age and early Iron Age culture of what is now Poland and its neighbours, from about 1300 to 500 BCE. The map shows it in 700 BCE.

It belonged to the wide Urnfield world: the dead were burned and their ashes buried in pottery urns, sometimes in cemeteries of thousands of graves. Its people farmed, raised animals and worked bronze, and later iron, which came in from the Hallstatt culture to the south. They traded along the Amber Road that carried Baltic amber to the Mediterranean.

Its best known site is Biskupin, a fortified village on a lake island, built in the 8th century BCE with rows of wooden houses inside a rampart of timber and earth. Many such forts appeared in this period. In the 6th and 5th centuries BCE the culture declined, perhaps under pressure from Scythian raids and the spread of the Pomeranian culture from the north. It followed earlier Bronze Age cultures such as Únětice.
